title: Optimization methods for large-scale machine learning
contribution: A SIAM Review survey (with Bottou and Curtis) that frames large-scale ML optimization around SG, gives one unified convergence and work-complexity theory for a generalized SG covering mini-batch and scaled (quasi-Newton) directions, and maps the next generation along two axes, noise reduction and second-order methods (arXiv v3 pp. 20-24, 34-37, 82).
problem_entry: Enters through the application field: three questions (p. 3) answered with two case studies, convex text classification on RCV1 and nonconvex DNNs (pp. 4-9), recast as expected vs empirical risk (pp. 9-15); the thesis is that classical nonlinear optimization typically falters in large-scale ML (p. 3).
key_idea: A two-axis map with SG at the origin (Fig. 3.3, p. 20) and one generalized SG (Algorithm 4.1, (4.2), p. 22) whose direction can be a stochastic gradient, a mini-batch gradient or Hk times one; classical engines are kept and only the noise-sensitive part is adapted: the Hessian is subsampled more lightly than the gradient (p. 53), and L-BFGS pairs are formed with the same seed or from decoupled Hessian-vector products every 10-20 iterations (SQN, pp. 57-59).
assumptions: L-smooth F (Assumption 4.1, p. 23); first- and second-moment limits with V[g] <= M + MV||grad F||^2 (Assumption 4.3, p. 24); strong convexity for all rates (Assumption 4.5, p. 26); independence of the seeds and results in expectation adopted for convenience (footnote 4, p. 22; Inset 4.2, p. 25); work complexity under the batch-favourable E ~ 1/n + eps (4.34, p. 36).
proof_devices: Two fundamental lemmas (expected descent, Lemma 4.2 p. 23; moment-bounded form, Lemma 4.4 p. 24) from which all results are derived (p. 23)
Contraction inequality after subtracting the asymptotic noise floor alpha*L*M/(2c*mu): linear convergence to a neighbourhood (Theorem 4.6, (4.15)-(4.16), pp. 26-27)
Heuristic step-halving schedule giving O(1/k) (pp. 27-28, (4.17)-(4.18), Fig. 4.1)
Induction on nu/(gamma+k) with beta > 1/(c*mu); constant (2/mu^2)(L/c)(M/c) exposes conditioning (Theorem 4.7, pp. 28-29; (4.24), p. 30)
Mini-batch vs simple SG compared through the constants M/nmb and the stepsize cap (pp. 30-31)

Nonconvex: telescoping and weighted sums (Theorems 4.8, 4.10, pp. 32-33), lim inf (Theorem 4.9, p. 33), random-iterate convergence in probability via Markov (Corollary 4.11, p. 34), S+/S- convergent-sum argument for a full limit (Corollary 4.12, proof p. 84)
Work-complexity macroscopic problem: error split Eapp + Eest + Eopt (4.31) under a time budget (4.32), Table 4.1 (pp. 35-37); noisy-oracle Omega(1/k) lower bound (pp. 36-37)
Geometric variance decay gives a linear rate by induction (Theorem 5.1, pp. 41-42); geometric-sum count of total sample gradients O(1/eps) for nk = ceil(tau^(k-1)) (Theorem 5.3, pp. 43-44)
Descent test ||g - grad F|| <= chi||g|| (5.11) estimated by a sample-variance test (5.12) with a geometric backup (p. 45)
Same descent-lemma template reused for randomized coordinate descent (Theorem 7.1, p. 72) and proximal gradient (Theorem 8.1, pp. 75-76)
One-line counterexample |w| rules out the minimum-norm subgradient as an inexactness measure; ISTA-step norm adopted (footnote 9 and text, p. 80)
experiments: One illustrative experiment only: batch L-BFGS vs SG (fixed alpha = 4, tuned by repeated runs) on RCV1 logistic regression, cost in accessed data points over 10 epochs (Fig. 3.1, pp. 17-18); benchmarking is declined to avoid test-set and implementation bias (p. 4); no test set, profiles or failure counts; other practical claims are cited (pp. 47, 65).
positioning: Against both communities: ML's view of SG as ideal is 'far from settled' (p. 40), while optimizers' batch preference is answered on intuitive, practical and theoretical grounds (pp. 15-19); historical credit to Robbins-Monro, Bertsekas, Bottou-Bousquet, Nemirovski-Yudin, Polyak-Juditsky (pp. 16-17, 35-37, 49); graded criticism, including of the group's own orthant code [30] (p. 82) and of general bound-constrained methods such as his own L-BFGS-B [163] (p. 78); 8 of 164 references have Nocedal as an author, none has Curtis; the SQN paragraph has no citation (p. 58).
writing: Question-driven structure (p. 3), case studies first, one schematic reused as a road map (pp. 20, 40, 51), insets for history and caveats (pp. 16, 25, 39), a Commentary per method family (pp. 37-38, 49, 81-82), 'what can be learned' paragraphs after theorems (pp. 29-31), costs given as numbers (4md, 20x SG, batch >= 20 or 50, pp. 54, 57), small explicit examples (pp. 17, 52, 66), local calibrated hedging (pp. 45, 49, 55, 68, 71).
limits_future: Synthesis and theory only (no new algorithm or software, p. 82); parallel/distributed, ADMM and EM not covered (p. 82); rates for strongly convex functions only (p. 25); open: rates of subsampled-Hessian Newton (p. 54), nonconvex Newton-CG (p. 55), stochastic quasi-Newton's potential (p. 58), momentum guarantees (p. 69), randomized CD in practice (p. 71); future: local-convexity adaptivity (p. 37), an SG-to-reduced-variance method (p. 45), noise reduction combined with second-order steps (pp. 21, 57).

method_links.note: SG, not his own L-BFGS, is put at the centre because the ML problem structure favours it, and Fig. 3.1 shows SG beating batch L-BFGS early; structure-exploiting choices are preferred, including ell1-specific gradient projection over general bound-constrained techniques such as his own L-BFGS-B [163]. Also case evidence for Heuristic 9: the group's methods appear only as cells of the field map.
Received wisdom on trial on both sides (ML: SG is ideal; optimization: batch is natural), but the trial is by theory and cost accounting, not by building and testing the dismissed simple option.

Same goal (methods, not implementations), reached by declining benchmarks to avoid test-set and implementation bias; the single plot discloses that the rival SG was tuned, but it is one problem called representative with no aggregate (against step 7's stop rule).

L-BFGS kept as the engine; the failing component (curvature pairs corrupted by noisy gradient differences, with lingering bad updates) is repaired by same-sample differences or decoupled Hessian-vector-product pairs; dynamic sampling uses an estimate-driven variance test with a geometric backup as recovery; Newton-CG keeps its line search with a subsampled Hessian.

Work-complexity analysis separates SG from batch gradient (Table 4.1) and from gradient aggregation, is checked against practice (Fig. 3.1), ties the bound to conditioning via (L/c)(M/c), and places quasi-Newton's benefit in the constant rather than the rate.

Tension with Taste warning sign 3 and IT5: the summary credits SG's success to its superior work complexity guarantees, i.e. complexity as the reason to prefer a method, though a large gap between asymptotics and practice is stated.

Weak: each method family closes with explicit open questions; any link from the p. 45 call for an SG-to-reduced-variance method to the group's later progressive-batching L-BFGS work (arXiv:1802.05374 in SKILL.md) is inferred from timing only, not checked.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Prove once for an abstract direction
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: One generalized SG whose direction is a parameter (stochastic, mini-batch, or Hk-scaled), with all theorems derived from two lemmas; the same descent-lemma template is reused for noise reduction, coordinate descent and proximal gradient.

Each enhancement is costed as a multiple of an SG iteration before any benefit is claimed: 4md (20x at m = 5), maxcg x factor x gcost + gcost, 2m + n per SVRG cycle, diagonal Gauss-Newton roughly twice SG.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Allocate sample accuracy by component tolerance
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: The Hessian sample is smaller than the gradient sample because the iteration tolerates Hessian noise more; curvature pairs are computed on a larger sample, less often.
The review explicitly declines numerical comparisons to avoid test-set and implementation bias and compares methods through work complexity and theory instead (Method 1 variant for review papers).

transferable: Write one generalized algorithm whose search direction is a parameter and derive every theorem from two lemmas (expected descent plus a second-moment bound), so one proof covers SG, mini-batch SG and stochastic quasi-Newton (pp. 22-24).

State the variance bound as M + MV||grad F||^2: fixed-step theorems then show a noise floor, M = 0 recovers deterministic rates, and M zeta^(k-1) gives linear rates for noise-reducing schemes (pp. 24, 26-27, 41-42).
Compare methods by total work to eps under a time budget using Eapp + Eest + Eopt, assuming the statistical rate most favourable to the rival, and show your method still wins (pp. 35-37).

Prove a growing-sample method efficient by counting total sample gradients with a geometric sum, and pair the adaptive variance test with a preset geometric backup so the theorem stays valid (pp. 43-45).

For stochastic quasi-Newton, form curvature pairs from a separate, larger sample (same seed at both points, or a subsampled Hessian-vector product) and refresh them every 10-20 iterations (pp. 57-58).
In subsampled Newton-CG, subsample the Hessian more lightly than the gradient and cap CG so that maxcg x factor is about 1, making a step cost about one SG step (pp. 53-54).
Price every enhancement in base-iteration units before arguing for it (4md vs d; 2m + n per SVRG cycle) (pp. 47, 57).
Choose an inexactness measure for a nonsmooth subproblem that vanishes exactly at the minimizer and varies continuously; test candidates on |w| (p. 80).
In an illustrative plot, count cost in a unit fair to both sides (accessed data points), disclose which side was tuned and say where the ranking reverses (pp. 17-19).
coauthors: Léon Bottou (Facebook AI Research), Frank E. Curtis (Lehigh ISE)

quotes.text: Rather than contrast SG and other methods based on the results of numerical experiments—which might bias our review toward a limited test set and implementation details—we focus our attention on fundamental computational trade-offs and theoretical properties of optimization methods.
have led many in the machine learning community to view SG as the ideal optimization approach for large-scale applications. We argue, however, that this is far from settled.
